appraisal_events.evidence: « ce pauvre homme, qui est une chère créature innocente, mais enfin qui a des idées de l'autre monde »; « Je me sens plus rapprochée, plus consanguine de mon cocher, de mes chevaux, que de cet homme »; « Cette pierre vivante a beau être mon cousin, elle me fait peur et je n'ai qu'une idée, c'est de la laisser dans son moyen âge. À part ça, je reconnais qu'il n'a jamais assassiné personne. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The bulk of the duchesse's speech is a sustained, image-rich mockery of Gilbert as an anachronistic medieval effigy, less kin to her than her coachman or her horses, closed by a mock-exculpation. The narrator reports the salon performance without commenting on Gilbert himself, but the diminishment of him is unmistakable and is the passage's dominant staged movement.

appraisal_events.evidence: « en ajoutant de plus en plus aux mots (qui étaient presque des mots de moi, car j'avais justement émis devant elle une idée analogue), grâce à sa prononciation, l'équivalent de ce que pour les caractères imprimés on appelle italiques »; « Je ne peux guère me citer, parce que moi, au contraire, j'ai toujours aimé dès le début toutes les manifestations intéressantes »; « comme dit mon beau-frère Palamède »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's parenthesis quietly reveals that the duchesse's italicized brilliance is his own borrowed idea, and the passage stacks a second borrowing from Palamède and a self-exempting boast about her own precocious taste that she immediately undercuts ("ce tableau que je n'aime pas tout"). Her rhetorical command remains real, but its originality is ironized.

status_effects.explanation: Gilbert is comprehensively ridiculed in absentia as a frightening living tombstone stranded in the Middle Ages, with even the concession that he has murdered no one working as a diminishment.
She holds the floor throughout, sets and defends her thesis ("qui tenait à son idée"), and dominates the exchange with vivid, quotable wit that the princesse can only follow.
The narrator's aside deflates the very originality her delivery advertises, showing her celebrated esprit to be assembled from other people's phrases and paired with a boast her own words contradict.

ambiguities: The final speaker is designated only as « le général » and is not named in the passage; his pointed refusal to smile or assent (« mais sans sourire ni adhérer aux plaisanteries de la duchesse ») functions as withheld endorsement of her wit, but since no name is given he is not listed among characters_present and no event is built on him.

The narrator's parenthesis (« qui étaient presque des mots de moi ») could be read as a neutral note of intellectual proximity rather than a deflation; the ironizing reading is taken here because it is reinforced by the second attributed borrowing from Palamède and by the duchesse's self-flattering claim of always having liked new things.
